newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Barefoot black in skins exorcises S.Africa's ghosts.
newsitem.headline: Barefoot black in skins exorcises S.Africa's ghosts.

text.p: The barefoot South African in animal skins who danced on the chairs in parliament on Friday showed just how thoroughly the apartheid dream of the country's former white rulers has been shattered.

The black man was among a stream of traditional praise singers who leapt and pranced through the old parliamentary chamber as part of the inauguration of South Africa's Council of Traditional Leaders, a statutory body with advisory powers intended as a political sop to the country's hereditary chiefs.
The ceremony took place in a room where South Africa's national assembly used to meet before the parliamentary complex was extended.

Troupes of women dancers in ochre body paint and jackal-skin bikinis gyrated to syncopated drumming and clapping, exorcising the ghosts of the gloomy wood-panelled chamber where generations of white-minority leaders passed the apartheid laws that made South Africa an inernational pariah.

Bare-chested warriors with shields and whips performed mock war dances and the leading praise singer sprang onto the green leather upholstered chairs where parliamentary officials used to preside, shaking his feathered headdress and swirling a fly whisk as he delivered a eulogy to President Nelson Mandela.

Mandela, in a sombre Western suit, referred in his speech to the irony of the country's chiefs meeting in the assembly where grim, elderly white men had once laboured to impose their rule on southern Africa.

"Almost 120 years (after the battle of Isandlwana) we gather in Cape Town... in the precincts of an institution that was used to... defeat, subjugate and dispossess the African people, to plunder their land and usurp its wealth," Mandela said.
The battle of Isandlwana, one of the proudest chapters in Zulu history, marked a rare defeat for imperial British soldiers by natives armed only with spears, clubs and shields.
"We meet in the full and fulfilling knowledge that we can now declare: The country is in the hands of the people," Mandela said.
He described the new council as constituting a branch of government which would serve the chiefs, rather than treat them as an anthropological curiosity.
"Our freedom is giving impetus to the recovery of our history... freeing our understanding of the past from the colonial account of our country and region," Mandela said.
